lead: Every emission control is a choice of place: stop the pollutant forming inside the cylinder, or convert and trap it in the exhaust line. In-cylinder methods change mixing, timing and temperature. After-treatment adds catalysts, filters and urea. Petrol engines near stoichiometric use a three-way catalyst; diesels run lean and need an oxidation catalyst, a particulate filter and SCR or a lean NOx trap. The skill is matching the device to the engine's air-fuel ratio and exhaust temperature, not buying the largest catalyst.
prereq: You need: 6.1 and 6.2 for where each pollutant is born, Unit 2 for injection and ignition timing, and Unit 3 for air motion and combustion chambers.

blocks.text: In-cylinder control keeps the pollutant from leaving the engine. For CI engines, retarding injection timing lowers peak flame temperature and so lowers NOx. It costs fuel and raises particulate matter (PM). Higher injection pressure and common rail make finer sprays, better mixing and less soot. Multiple injection splits one pulse into pilot, main and post pulses. A pilot softens ignition; a post pulse late in expansion adds fuel for DPF regeneration or reduces soot. Injection rate shaping changes how fast fuel enters; a slow start lowers NOx and noise. Chamber and swirl design, from Unit 3, shorten the rich core where soot grows. For SI engines, spark retard lowers NOx but costs power; closed-loop stoichiometric control uses a lambda sensor to hold λ = actual AFR ÷ stoichiometric AFR near 1. Water injection cools the charge and lowers NOx. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) sends exhaust back to the intake. It dilutes oxygen, adds CO2 and H2O that absorb heat (thermal effect), and changes reaction chemistry; together these lower NOx. Hot EGR is simple but less dense; cooled EGR packs more mass for the same volume. High-pressure EGR takes gas before the turbine; low-pressure EGR takes it after the DPF and needs a cleaner path. EGR raises PM and fuel use if overdone. Two small lines: crankcase ventilation routes blow-by gas back to the intake; an evaporative canister traps fuel vapour from the tank and purges it at the right moment.

sections.h3: After-treatment: three-way catalyst and diesel line

blocks.text: After-treatment treats the gas after the exhaust valve. The three-way catalytic converter (TWC) is for stoichiometric petrol engines. It carries platinum, palladium and rhodium. At λ≈1 it runs three reactions: CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (CO is carbon monoxide), HC + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (HC is unburnt hydrocarbon), and CO + NO → ½N₂ + CO₂ (NO is nitric oxide, part of NOx). The window is narrow, about λ = 0.99 to 1.00 (a few tenths of an air-fuel ratio around 14.7:1 for petrol). A lambda sensor and closed loop keep the mixture there; with spare O₂ the NO reaction stops, with excess fuel the oxidation reactions stop. The diesel line is different because diesel is always lean. The diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC) oxidises CO and HC and turns NO into NO₂, which helps the next devices. The diesel particulate filter (DPF) is a wall-flow honeycomb: alternate channel ends are blocked, so gas passes through porous walls and soot stays. Passive regeneration burns soot with NO₂; active regeneration uses a late post-injection to raise temperature. Ash remains and slowly blocks the filter. Selective catalytic reduction (SCR) injects urea solution, AdBlue, 32.5% urea in water. It decomposes to ammonia. The standard reaction is 4NH₃ + 4NO + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O. A fast SCR route also uses NO₂. Light-off is near 200 °C, and too much ammonia causes ammonia slip. The lean NOx trap (LNT) stores NOx as barium nitrate while lean, then a short rich purge reduces it. Sulphur poisons the LNT.

Choose by air-fuel ratio first. A stoichiometric petrol engine gets a TWC and a lambda sensor. A lean-burn petrol or diesel gets a DOC, then either SCR with urea or an LNT. A DPF is standard on the modern diesel; a gasoline particulate filter (GPF) is added to petrol where PM is regulated. SCR needs a supply of AdBlue and a warm exhaust; LNT avoids urea but suffers sulphur poisoning and needs rich purges. A DPF is not optional on a modern diesel if PM is regulated. The devices act in order: DOC, DPF, urea mixer, SCR. The DOC makes NO₂ for DPF and SCR. The DPF removes soot but its regeneration costs fuel. The SCR removes NOx but can slip ammonia. The LNT stores NOx but needs a rich purge.

examples.question: An EGR valve opens on a diesel engine. CO₂ is 0.04% in the ambient air, 1.80% in the intake and 12.0% in the exhaust. Find the EGR percentage.
steps: Write the CO₂-based EGR formula: EGR% = [(CO₂ intake − CO₂ ambient) ÷ (CO₂ exhaust − CO₂ intake)] × 100.
Round to one decimal place: 17.3. The formula divides by the intake CO₂, so 17.3 is the recirculated exhaust mass per 100 parts of fresh air.
examples.answer: The CO₂ formula gives 17.3 parts of recirculated exhaust per 100 parts of fresh air. As a fraction of the intake charge itself, the exhaust is (1.76 ÷ 11.96) × 100 = 14.7%.

traps: Fitting a three-way catalyst to a lean-burn or diesel engine. The TWC needs λ within about ±0.01 of 1 (roughly ±0.2 in air-fuel ratio around 14.7:1); spare O₂ blocks NOx reduction and excess fuel blocks CO and HC oxidation.
Thinking EGR always saves fuel. EGR lowers NOx but raises PM and fuel use if overdone; cooled EGR also adds a cooler load.
Confusing the DOC and the DPF. The DOC oxidises gases; the DPF traps solid soot.
Forgetting DPF ash. Regeneration burns soot, not ash; ash stays and slowly blocks the filter.

Using the CO₂ EGR formula as an exhaust mass fraction. The formula divides by (CO₂ exhaust − CO₂ intake), so the answer is a ratio of recirculated exhaust to fresh air, not a fraction of the exhaust flow.

quiz.q: What does a three-way catalytic converter convert?
quiz.a: It converts CO, HC and NOx into CO₂, H₂O and N₂ by three reactions near λ=1.

quiz.q: Why does EGR lower NOx but raise PM?
quiz.a: EGR dilutes O₂ and adds heat-absorbing CO₂ and H₂O, so flame temperature falls. Less oxygen and lower temperature also slow soot burn-out, so PM rises.

quiz.q: A diesel has CO₂ 0.04% ambient, 1.50% intake and 10.0% exhaust. Find EGR%.
quiz.a: EGR% = [(1.50 − 0.04) ÷ (10.0 − 1.50)] × 100 = (1.46 ÷ 8.50) × 100 = 17.2 parts of exhaust per 100 parts of fresh air. As a fraction of the intake charge, (1.46 ÷ 9.96) × 100 = 14.7%.

quiz.q: Why does a TWC fail on a lean diesel?
quiz.a: Spare O₂ prevents NO reduction, and lean exhaust cannot supply enough reductant. NOx passes. Such engines need DOC, DPF and SCR or an LNT.

quiz.q: SCR uses 32.5% urea solution. What mass of urea is in 10 kg AdBlue?
quiz.a: Urea mass = 0.325 × 10 kg = 3.25 kg; water mass = 6.75 kg.
Ammonia slip is unreacted NH₃ leaving the SCR catalyst.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production lines add a diesel oxidation catalyst, a coated DPF, a urea mixer and an SCR, with sensors for NOx, temperature and ammonia. Real calibration uses engine maps and on-board diagnostics; a faulty EGR valve or a low AdBlue tank can force a torque limit. Researchers are testing electrically heated catalysts and close-coupled SCR for cold starts. Search for 'BS-VI after-treatment', 'DPF regeneration strategy' and 'ammonia slip control'.
